blocks.text: Roxanne asked if I wanted coffee before I threatened to take her job. She was standing by the glass conference room door with her mug in one hand, and I was already angry enough that I didn’t answer her.
I told my daughter I’d fire her and make sure nobody in Kentucky hired her if she made Jessica leave her house.
I said it in front of half the marketing department. I know how that sounds. I did it anyway.

I’m Marcus. I own a furniture company in Louisville, and Roxanne was thirty and running our marketing department. I used to tell people she was the most capable person in the building. That afternoon, I made clear I thought being capable still meant she belonged to me.

The reason I was there started with Jessica’s phone call three months before. I remember the exact hour because the clock over my desk had stopped at , and I kept meaning to fix it. Jessica was crying. Her marriage had lasted less than six months, and her husband had told her to leave after another fight about money.
I asked if she’d called Roxanne. I knew the answer before Jessica said yes. I told Jessica that Roxanne had a spare room and that family helped family.
I didn’t call Roxanne first. I told myself it would be easier if Jessica arrived and explained.
I’ve said that kind of thing all my life. It sounds like a small shortcut. It wasn’t. I was giving away someone else’s time, space, and patience because I didn’t want to hear my older daughter cry.

Roxanne owned a modest house in Louisville. She’d bought it with years of savings, and she liked things kept in their place. Not fancy things. Just the keys on the little table by the door, the bills in the same drawer, the quiet after work. I knew that about Roxanne. I also knew Jessica hated being told no.
Jessica showed up two days later with a moving truck. I didn’t see the truck myself, but Roxanne called me that night.
I asked what that meant. Roxanne said movers had brought clothes, shoes, racks, boxes, and enough handbags to fill the guest room twice.
Jessica had already said she wanted Roxanne’s bedroom because the guest room didn’t have enough room for her skincare things.
Roxanne went quiet. I thought I’d helped. Then she said, “I did. She slammed the door.”

I should have asked whether Jessica had apologized. I should have asked whether Roxanne wanted her there at all. Instead, I said the divorce had rattled Jessica and that it would settle down. I had spent years treating Jessica’s feelings like emergencies and Roxanne’s boundaries like inconveniences. I wasn’t going to change that in one phone call.

For the first couple weeks, I heard little complaints from Roxanne. Dishes. Takeout cartons. Jessica stretched on the sofa. Jessica asking what they were having for dinner as if Roxanne had staff. I told myself those were normal things between sisters. That was convenient, because I didn’t live there.
Roxanne kept the peace. Jessica had always been good at asking for care in a way that made refusal sound cruel.
She’d had a hard marriage, I said. She was starting over, I said. I didn’t say that Roxanne had been starting over too, in her own house, with somebody else’s mess on the kitchen counter.

One night Roxanne called after finding the living room painted pink. Jessica had hired someone to repaint every wall while Roxanne was at work. Roxanne’s framed art was in the garage beside the trash cans. The frames were chipped. One canvas was leaning against a damp wall.

I heard the words but didn’t picture it. I was looking at a delivery schedule when Roxanne said she’d come home to strangers in the kitchen, music playing, food taken from her refrigerator, and Jessica pouring Roxanne’s wine.
I asked whether Jessica had said it was an accident. Roxanne said Jessica called the walls boring and told her wine was meant to be enjoyed. Then Roxanne said she’d made the guests leave.

I remember being relieved that Roxanne hadn’t yelled. That’s the part I feel bad about now. Not that I’d failed to protect her. That I was glad she’d managed the problem without making trouble for me.
The next morning, I called Jessica. I told her she had to respect Roxanne’s house. Jessica said Roxanne had humiliated her in front of friends.
“Then pay for the paint and the art frames,” I said.

Jessica told me she had no money. She said her husband was holding up the divorce settlement and she needed a little breathing room. I said I’d talk to Roxanne. I didn’t tell Jessica she had to move out.
I thought I could keep both daughters from being angry at me by making Roxanne wait. That was my plan. It was a bad one, but I kept using it.

Roxanne had given Jessica a supplementary credit card, with a limit of $5,000, for groceries and things around the house. Roxanne called it a practical choice. I figured the limit was high because Jessica’s groceries were expensive. I didn’t ask what “things around the house” meant. I didn’t want another argument.

Then Jessica used the card for clothes, a $300 lunch, and a day at a spa. The charges added up to $5,183 in fewer than ten days. I found out because Roxanne called me at work, and her voice had gone flat.
I asked whether Jessica had talked to her about it. Roxanne said Jessica was in bed when she saw the declined-card alert. Roxanne had gone in and asked her to pay it back.
“She said she needed to feel like herself.”
I heard that sentence and knew it wasn’t an answer. I also knew what I was going to do. I was going to call Jessica, hear her cry, and find a reason to tell Roxanne to give her more time.
Roxanne said she’d told Jessica to move out. Jessica called me right after and said Roxanne was putting her on the street over food.
“Dad, I can’t stay with her if she hates me.”

I asked what happened with the card. Jessica said Roxanne had given it to her, and she’d assumed it was okay to use. Jessica didn’t mention the spa until I asked. Then she said the settlement would come through soon.

I wanted to believe her. I wanted to believe my younger daughter was scared, not selfish. Maybe she was both. I still had the chance to tell Jessica to repay the money and leave. Instead, I got in my car and drove to the office.

I went straight past reception and called Roxanne’s name. People looked up from their desks. I saw her get up, and I could have taken a breath. I could have asked to speak somewhere private. Instead, I put a hand on her arm and told her to come into the conference room.
I remember the smell of coffee from her mug. It was burnt, the way it gets when somebody leaves it on the warmer too long. She set it down and asked what Jessica had told me.
I said Jessica was vulnerable and that Roxanne couldn’t throw her out over a credit card. Roxanne unlocked her phone and held up the statement.
I said I didn’t care whether Roxanne was right or wrong. Jessica was her sister. I told her she had to take care of family.

Roxanne said it was her house and her money. She said the pink walls were still there. She said the artwork was in the garage. She said strangers had been in her home and she’d been cleaning up after them.

I didn’t look at the statement. I didn’t want to read the details because the details were not the problem I had come to solve. I wanted Roxanne to agree and let me leave with my idea of myself intact.
So I told her I owned the company. I said I’d given her a good position. I said no other employer in Kentucky would hire her if I called around.
I said those things because I knew they would hurt. I knew her job mattered. I knew she’d worked for that position. And I used it to get what I wanted.

Roxanne looked at me for a long time. Through the glass, I could see people pretending to work. She didn’t cry. She didn’t shout. She picked up her coffee, took a sip, and made a face because it was cold.
“You’re threatening your own daughter over Jessica’s spending?”

I said I was trying to keep the family together. That wasn’t true, or not the whole truth. I was trying to keep Jessica from being angry with me. I was trying to keep Roxanne available as the person who would absorb the mess.
Roxanne asked if I was finished. I said she needed to think about what she was doing. Then I walked out. I left the glass door open behind me.

The next few days, nobody at work said anything about the conference room. That didn’t mean nobody had heard. My office manager, Darlene, asked if I needed the marketing meeting moved. I told her no. I didn’t know what else to say.

Roxanne kept showing up. She answered emails, sat in meetings, and sent the weekly campaign report before noon. She didn’t come into my office. At home, she stopped answering my calls. I told myself she was cooling off.
Jessica said Roxanne was punishing the whole family. I told Jessica she needed to give Roxanne time. That sounded reasonable until Jessica asked if she could use another card.
She started crying. I didn’t change my answer, but I also didn’t tell her she had to leave Roxanne’s house. I was still hoping Roxanne would make the hard decision for me.

A week after the conference room, I got home and found Jessica at my kitchen table with a notebook. She’d written down what she thought she was owed from the divorce, what she wanted to buy, and where she might stay if the settlement came through. She told me she’d already applied for two jobs.
I said I hadn’t asked her to. Jessica told me Roxanne had always resented her. I almost agreed. It was easy, and I’d used that explanation before.
Then Jessica said, “She doesn’t know how hard it is to start over.”
I asked whether Jessica had called Roxanne to apologize. Jessica stopped writing.
Jessica closed the notebook. I thought I’d finally made the point. But she said she couldn’t apologize for needing help. I told her that wasn’t the same thing as spending money without permission.

Jessica said the card had been offered. I told her it was for groceries. She said she’d bought food too. She didn’t mention the $300 lunch or the spa. We sat there with the notebook between us, and I understood Jessica had learned from me that if she sounded hurt enough, the facts could wait.

I called Roxanne that night. She didn’t answer. I left a message asking her to let Jessica stay until the divorce papers were done. I started to say I was sorry for what I’d said at work, but I stopped before the words came out. I said we’d talk soon.
Roxanne texted the next morning: “I’m handling it.”
